meeting_header: Date: 2026-08-19 | Start: 15:30 UTC | Duration: 62 minutes\nLocation: Zoom | Recording: enabled\nAttendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood CSM); Sarah Lin (CISO, Northgate), Carlos Mejia (Cloud Architect), Priya Rao (Compliance Lead), Ethan Brooks (SRE)
summary: Redwood walked Northgate through encryption-at-rest/in-transit options, BYOK and HSM connector capabilities, and residency/escrow implications. Customer is evaluating a hybrid approach: Private deployment inside their VPC with HSM-backed keys for regulated telemetry and billing data. Key questions remain around network connectivity (no inbound), HSM models supported (on-prem vs cloud HSM), key rotation cadence, and audit log retention for SOC2 purposes. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share architecture doc, SOC2/ISO attestations, and PoC proposal; customer to share network topology and residency list.
topics: Encryption at rest vs in transit overview
On-prem HSM connectivity (outbound-only) and proxy model
Audit logs and evidence for SOC2/ISO
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll use the next hour to run through how Redwood handles keys, BYOK options, and our HSM connector patterns. I know Northgate has some residency constraints. Sarah: yes that's right, we've got some state-level regs for billing PII.

[00:00:28] Sarah (Northgate): Sorry I jumped on a little late, appreciate you doing this. Our main ask is we need to keep certain datasets within state X data centers and HSM-backed keys for those stores. Can you do per-dataset residency?

[00:00:45] Liam (Redwood): Short answer: yes, we support routing and per-bucket model pinning. Long answer: we'll walk through policy routing and the Private deployment pattern where keys can be customer-managed.

[00:01:12] Carlos (Northgate): Quick context: our stack is multi-cloud, primary is Azure, and we've got an on-prem colocation for the billing DB. Our security posture requires no inbound connections to the colocation. So any HSM connector would need to originate from the colo or use a proxy.

[00:01:38] Liam (Redwood): Understood. We have an outbound-only connector pattern: an agent in your network establishes an outbound TLS tunnel to Redwood control plane for key provisioning and wrapping operations. No inbound ports required. There are a few ways we do key wrapping — we can either import wrapped keys (BYOK) or do remote key usage with key material never leaving the HSM.

[00:02:05] Priya (Northgate): When you say "wrap" — is that the same as key import? We have compliance rules about key escrow and escrow policies.

[00:02:15] Maya (Redwood): Good callout. There's some terminology mismatch sometimes. BYOK import means you generate the key material in your HSM and import a wrapped key into Redwood's key store. With HSM-backed remote uses (we call it "KMaaS bridge" in some docs) the key stays in your HSM and Redwood sends ciphertext to be unwrapped or signs inside the HSM via the connector. We can support both models depending on your control requirement.

[00:02:48] Ethan (Northgate): Can you support nCipher and AWS CloudHSM? Our colo runs Thales/nCipher HW and our cloud dev environment uses CloudHSM.

[00:02:58] Liam (Redwood): We support common PKCS#11 HSMs and CloudHSM via a connector. For nCipher we have an adapter; for Thales it's a little more manual but supported. I'll put a compatibility matrix in the doc.

[00:03:18] Carlos: Important: any key usage must be logged in a way we can export for SOC2 audits. We need immutable audit trails for key creation, rotation, wrap/unwrap events. What's the retention and export format?

[00:03:33] Jordan (Redwood): Our audit logs are pushed to the customer's logging sink (S3/Blob/GCS or SIEM) and retained per policy. The default retention in Redwood is 90 days unless you request longer retention. Exports can be provided as newline-delimited JSON with signatures for integrity.

[00:03:56] Sarah: Does that include KMS admin operations — e.g., key policy changes, RBAC grants, SAML provisioning events? We need proof for SOC2 Type II.

[00:04:07] Maya: Yes we capture admin operations, who changed them via SSO identity (SAML/SCIM tie-in), and we record the before/after for critical policy changes. We can generate audit bundles for auditors.

[00:04:26] Priya: Any caveats about tamper-proofing logs? We need write-once-read-many (WORM) or signed logs for auditors.

[00:04:34] Liam: We provide log signing via an append-only log with HMAC chaining, and you can also ship to your WORM storage. For very sensitive cases we recommend a chained signing workflow — we'll include the workflow in the design doc.

[00:04:55] Carlos: Network — how does the connector authenticate? We cannot accept inbound IAM or token pushes. We need mutual TLS with client certs and IP whitelisting outbound.

[00:05:05] Liam: Connector initiates outbound mutual TLS using client certs that we provision alongside the connector certificate. Auth is mutual TLS plus shorter-lived tokens for per-request authorization. IP whitelisting is supported on the control plane side.

[00:05:24] Ethan: Is the connector open source or closed? We'll have to run some code review for supply chain.

[00:05:31] Maya: The connector is a small agent; we provide a reference build and we can give you a vetted binary and a reproducible build script. For very strict requirements we can offer a source review process.

[00:05:46] Sarah: Rotation policy — we've got a policy: key rotation every 180 days for data-encryption keys, and master keys yearly, unless there's an incident. Can Redwood automate rotation and coordinate with our HSM?

[00:05:58] Liam: Yes. For imported keys we can schedule rotation events but the rotation itself either triggers a new key import from your HSM, or if using remote key operations, rotation occurs inside the HSM and Redwood polls and syncs the new key metadata. We'll show flows for both in the doc.

[00:06:22] Priya: What about cross-region access when we have to keep residency? Suppose the model inference happens outside the state — can we do partial residency so only decryption must happen in-state?

[00:06:34] Maya: That pattern is common: keep the key operations in-residency and keep encrypted artifacts portable. Redwood supports routing by policy so requests requiring in-state key ops are routed to Private instances inside your region or to a dedicated HSM connector in the colo.

[00:06:52] Carlos: Are there latency implications if the inference model is in a managed hosted pool but the decryption happens in-state? That's relevant for real-time billing flows.

[00:07:04] Liam: Yes, you will see additional RTT for any round-trip to the HSM. We typically recommend caching wrapped keys or doing prefix caching so that the per-token latency isn't dominated by key ops. For PKI operations that require on-demand unwrapping, you should budget for tens to low hundreds of ms depending on location. We'll provide numbers from benchmarks.

[00:07:28] Ethan: About caching — what about key material never leaving HSM? Can you cache wrapped artifacts instead of plaintext keys?

[00:07:39] Liam: Exactly — we use wrapped key material stored in Redwood but the unwrap operation is delegated to your HSM via the connector. That lets you keep master keys secure while still getting performance benefits.

[00:07:55] Sarah: For auditors we also need to show key destruction and end-of-life. If a HSM is decommissioned how do we prove key destruction?

[00:08:05] Maya: HSM vendors provide tamper-evidence and zeroization logs. In addition, Redwood can record a key-destruction event with signed evidence and the HSM's serial number. We'll include a sample zeroization attestation in the artifacts pack.

[00:08:22] Priya: Data classification: we need to map datasets to residency and to key policy. Is that a manual mapping or can Redwood integrate with our CMDB?

[00:08:33] Jordan (Redwood): We can consume a simple CSV or integrate with CMDBs via API. Initially customers usually do a manual mapping for the PoC and then automate once policies stabilize.

[00:08:44] Carlos: SSO integration: we use Okta and SAML. We want RBAC for key ops. Can you bind key admin roles to Okta groups and restrict sign/decrypt to specific roles?

[00:08:55] Liam: Yes. We support SAML and SCIM for provisioning. RBAC policies can be scoped to keys, projects, or roles. You can require MFA on admin operations as well.

[00:09:10] Sarah: Any certifications we should be aware of? Do you have SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001? Also FIPS 140-2/3 support for HSMs?

[00:09:19] Maya: Redwood has SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 attestation — I'll attach the reports. For FIPS, we rely on the underlying HSM certification: CloudHSM and common HSMs are FIPS-capable; Redwood runtime can run on FIPS-enabled kernels in private deployments.

[00:09:38] Priya: Can you provide redacted copies for our auditors?

[00:09:42] Maya: Yes, we'll share redacted attestations and the compliance pack.

[00:09:49] Carlos: Practical question: if we bring keys from our HSM (BYOK), how many keys can be managed? We're looking at thousands of per-tenant keys for meter-level encryption.

[00:10:01] Liam: Scalability is governed by metadata store rather than HSM limits — HSMs are for master keys and signing. For data-encryption keys you typically use envelope encryption: a per-blob data key is wrapped by a master key. Redwood's platform is designed to manage millions of wrapped keys; the heavy ops don't hit the HSM except for master key operations.

[00:10:26] Ethan: If a tenant deletes data, do you have a mechanism to cascade delete wrapped keys and logs? We have e-discovery windows.

[00:10:35] Jordan: We support key lifecycle policies tied to object lifecycle. When data is deleted and the customer requests key deletion, we can rotate or retire the wrapping key and provide deletion attestations. We'll add the deletion flow to the PoC runbook.

[00:10:52] Sarah: Any constraints around hardware HSM firmware updates or service windows? We need to know if Redwood will manage connector updates or if that's on us.

[00:11:03] Liam: Connector updates are typically customer-controlled; we publish agent releases and security advisories. For Private deployments we can offer managed updates as part of an enterprise support bundle.

[00:11:16] Priya: On the legal side, is there a data processing addendum for key control and residency promises? Our legal team will need contractual language about not accessing plaintext and about key escrow exceptions.

[00:11:28] Maya: We have a DPA and a BYOK appendix that covers non-access and escrows. We also have options for key escrow with mutually agreed triggers (e.g., court order, subpoena) — we'll surface the clauses and proposed wording.

[00:11:42] Carlos: Can you walk through a sample flow — inference request that needs to touch a billing key in colocated HSM?

[00:11:49] Liam: Sure. High-level: 1) App calls Redwood API with encrypted payload; 2) Redwood route sees policy requiring in-colo decryption; 3) request routed to Private instance in colocation (or to Redwood control plane that forwards wrapped key op to your HSM connector); 4) HSM unwraps/cryptoperforms and returns tokenized response. We have diagrams — we'll include both routing and fallback (if HSM unavailable) flows.

[00:12:21] Sarah: What's your recommendation for fallback? Do you ever recommend a soft-fail that uses a hosted fallback key?

[00:12:30] Maya: We generally recommend fail-closed for regulated data: if HSM is unavailable, fail the operation. For non-critical use cases you can configure automatic fallback to a warmed substitute key in a nearby Redwood Private node, but that has regulatory tradeoffs.

[00:12:47] Priya: Auditors might want to see proof of that fail-closed behavior. Can you simulate outage scenarios as part of PoC?

[00:12:54] Liam: Yes, PoC runbook includes fault injection tests and audit collection for those scenarios.

[00:13:05] Carlos: Latency bench request: can Redwood run a test from our colo to an in-state Private instance and provide p95 latency numbers for unwrap/sign?

[00:13:13] Maya: Absolutely — we'll set up a bench plan; we'll need a connector in your colo and ephemeral test keys. We'll coordinate timing for minimal production impact.

[00:13:24] Ethan: On billing, if we use dedicated capacity + private HSM, what's the rough cost delta vs hosted? We need estimates for cloud budget planning.

[00:13:33] Maya: We'll include a pricing sketch in the PoC doc: dedicated reserved capacity + private deployment + managed connector has a premium, but the unit per-token cost for heavy throughput is lower. I'll send a spreadsheet with scenarios.

[00:13:46] Sarah: A couple of nitty-gritty items: key escrow — do you have multi-party escrow options? We want the ability to split escrow keys between legal and security.

[00:13:58] Liam: Yes, we support split-escrow or Shamir-like schemes. We can configure escrow to require multiple parties and thresholds. We'll explain operational tradeoffs.

[00:14:12] Priya: What about evidence for auditors around RBAC changes? We need to show who approved changes.

[00:14:18] Jordan: Approvals can be workflowed via integrations; we can tie RBAC policy changes to Jira/Confluence approvals and add that metadata to audit bundles.

[00:14:28] Carlos: Are there any data residency compliance gotchas you've seen? For example, cross-border telemetry or model telemetry that accidentally leaks region tags?

[00:14:38] Liam: Yes — metadata and logs often leak residency through region tags. We suggest scrubbing or routing telemetry to in-region sinks and making sure model telemetry is redacted or routed by policy. We'll include a checklist.

[00:14:53] Sarah: Okay let's recap. We'll need: architecture doc with connector details and supported HSMs, SOC2/ISO attestations, PoC runbook with bench tests and failover scenarios, pricing sheet, and legal BYOK appendix. On our side we'll provide: network topology, list of in-scope datasets and residency boundaries, and a small staging HSM for the PoC.

[00:15:17] Maya: That matches our notes. We'll send artifacts within three business days. Any other questions?

[00:15:25] Priya: One small thing — backup keys. If you replicate metadata to other regions for HA, how is key material protected?

[00:15:33] Liam: Only metadata and wrapped keys are replicated. Master key material never leaves the HSM unless you choose import. We'll document geographic replication controls.

[00:15:45] Carlos: Competitor note — we looked at CloudVendorX and VaultCorp; their agents require inbound tunnels which is a dealbreaker for our colo. Your outbound-only approach is attractive.

[00:15:58] Maya: Good to hear. We'll highlight that pattern in the doc.

[00:16:05] Sarah: Great. Thanks everyone. Wrap up?

[00:16:09] Maya: Wrap: we'll send the doc pack, schedule a pilot kickoff for next week if that works for you, and Liam will produce the HSM compatibility matrix.

[00:16:18] Sarah: Next week works. I'll circle back with legal if they need anything pre-signed.

[00:16:25] Maya: Awesome. Thanks all. End of recording.

Note: transcription contains occasional mis-hears (e.g., "KMaaS bridge" referred to as "K M as bridge" earlier), and speaker turns may overlap. Links referenced: (1) HSM connector design doc (link to be sent), (2) SOC2 + ISO pack (link to be sent), (3) PoC runbook (link to be sent).
